🪨💧 𝗖𝗮𝗻 𝘄𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝗲 𝗵𝘆𝗱𝗿𝗼𝗴𝗲𝗻 𝗯𝘆 𝗶𝗻𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗸?

Hydrogen is already manufactured worldwide for refining and fertilisers. But 𝗴𝗲𝗼𝗹𝗼𝗴𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗵𝘆𝗱𝗿𝗼𝗴𝗲𝗻 is different: H₂ can occur naturally underground.

The IEA (2026) reports exploration in almost 30 countries, but only one operating natural-H₂ well, in Mali. Meanwhile, Setiawan et al. (2026) documented H₂-rich gas seeps in Central Sulawesi, Indonesia.

A gas seep is not proof of an economically producible reservoir.

Now researchers are investigating something different: 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝘄𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗺𝘂𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗵𝘆𝗱𝗿𝗼𝗴𝗲𝗻 𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗸 𝗶𝘁𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳?

One emerging approach is 𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝘀𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.

Under suitable conditions, water reacts with iron-bearing minerals in ultramafic rocks. Oxidation of ferrous iron can generate molecular hydrogen (H₂).

The geological process is established. Engineering it for sustained hydrogen production is a different challenge.

🔹 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹.

Xia et al. (2026) experimentally demonstrated hydrogen generation during peridotite serpentinization. Time-lapse X-ray CT revealed serpentine growth along existing veins and associated rock-volume expansion.

🔹 𝗕𝘂𝘁 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘆𝗲𝘁 𝗮 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗼𝗶𝗿.

Hydrogen generation requires reactive minerals, water access, suitable temperature, and favorable reaction kinetics.

Christiansen et al. (2026) showed that natural H₂ generation can be strongly limited by reaction kinetics and dissolved-hydrogen saturation—constraints also relevant to engineered systems.

Meanwhile, mineral alteration can modify pore and fracture networks, potentially changing permeability and limiting sustained fluid circulation.

🔹 𝗖𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗶𝗻𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝘆 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿?

Eslami et al. (2026) modeled hydrogen generation in a fractured ultramafic reservoir. Cyclic injection improved modeled hydrogen production per unit of injected water under certain conditions, although continuous injection yielded more hydrogen overall.

This highlights the importance of coupled fluid flow, geochemistry, heat transfer, and rock-property evolution.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗮: Instead of only searching for naturally accumulated hydrogen, future subsurface engineering might also investigate how to stimulate its generation.

But laboratory hydrogen generation is not proof of economically recoverable production. Reaction rates, fluid access, gas recovery, reservoir evolution, and energy requirements remain major uncertainties.

In design class, first year of uni, I opened Microsoft Paint.
The classmate next to me laughed and asked why I wasn’t using Photoshop.

Later, when I wanted to customise my own website, I taught myself HTML and CSS.

Putri Karunia’s start sounds familiar. She was a girl in Indonesia with a Photoshop she couldn’t afford, learning HTML. I’m from Malaysia. Neither of us had the “right” tools, so we both learned a bit of code.

Today she’s the founder of Lunagraph, a design canvas that writes real React code. She says her first animation drafts are “around 80 to 85% done” by the time she wakes up: one agent designs overnight, a second one reviews.

I asked her how. The gist, for your own design process:
→ Start from your real product and design system, not a blank canvas
→ Ask for a few variations, then point at what you like in A and B
→ Ask for a dial (“a control for the speed”), not adjectives like “a bit slower”
→ Teach it your taste: saved references plus a storyline-first skill
→ Keep your code base clean, because agents copy the mess too

One limit: no logo (vector) editing yet, so logos still belong in Figma.

My takeaway: you don’t need the “right” tool to start. You need a real screen and a few good questions.

Thank you Putri for sharing your process 🙏

Challenge for Every City in the World: Waste Management and Urgent Need of Clean Energy

Cities and industries around the world face a dual crisis: escalating municipal solid waste and urgent need also for reliable, clean energy. Traditional waste-to-energy systems often struggle with high-moisture municipal waste and generate heavy emissions.

At BioCom Indonesia, we are engineering closed-loop infrastructure to turn municipal waste management into a continuous, zero-waste clean hydrogen engine.

Here is how our 3-stage integrated system works:

1. Hydrothermal Carbonization (HTC)

Mixed wet and dry municipal waste enters an Inconel pressurized thermal reactor without requiring energy-intensive pre-drying. Under controlled heat and pressure, organic and carbon-rich waste converts rapidly into energy-dense hydrochar (C).

2. Hydrochar Gasification

The resulting hydrochar moves into a high-temperature gasification unit, converting solid carbon into clean syngas—primarily carbon monoxide (CO) andhydrogen (H₂).

3. Perpetual Steam-Iron Process (Fe / Fe₃O₄)

Using a porous bed of iron and magnetite pellets, steam reacts with iron (Fe) to release high-purity green hydrogen gas (H₂) while forming magnetite (Fe₃O₄). The CO produced in Stage 2 is looped back into the reactor to reduce Fe₃O₄ back into elemental Fe—allowing the hydrogen generation cycle to repeat perpetually in a closed material loop.

By combining modular waste carbonization with chemical-looping hydrogen production, we can achieve99.8% mass balance efficiency and75%+ embodied carbon reduction—transforming urban waste liabilities into scalable clean energy assets.

Will the Next Inflation Shock Start on the Farm?

The next inflation shock may not begin at the petrol pump. It could emerge months later in the fields as farmers grapple with constrained fertilizer supplies, elevated diesel costs, and a strong El Niño just as planting and application decisions lock in.

Key points from the article:

- Energy markets react instantly; agriculture runs on a seasonal calendar. Higher input costs today show up as lower yields and tighter supplies later.
- Fertilizer is the quiet bottleneck: ~47% of traded sulfur (critical for phosphate) normally moves through the Strait of Hormuz. Sulfur prices spiked hard, major producers like Mosaic cut guidance, and farmers in key markets are expected to apply significantly less.
- Diesel is another squeeze, the Middle East and Russia normally account for half of global net diesel exports, and prices have roughly doubled since the conflict began.
- Biofuel mandates (e.g., Indonesia’s palm oil biodiesel) add competing demand for agricultural feedstocks.
- A very strong El Niño (>90% probability of a strong event) arrives while crops may be under-fertilized and less resilient.
- FAO Food Price Index already hit its highest since late 2022; cereals are up sharply year-on-year. The lagged effects could feed into protein costs, hit lower-income countries hardest, and complicate central-bank easing.

None of this makes a full-blown food crisis inevitable, markets adapt, but headline commodity prices alone are a poor guide. Watch fertilizer availability, sulfur and phosphate flows, diesel exports, planting decisions, and yield revisions.
